title: Paying fishers to save sharks killed more sharks
gist: The first marine conservation RCT (Booth et al., 2025) found that paying Indonesian fishers to release hammerhead and wedgefish alive backfired: fishers fished harder for over-priced wedgefish and ended up killing more critically endangered hammerheads.

insights.claim: Paying Indonesian fishers to release hammerhead sharks alive increased hammerhead retention, killing more critically endangered sharks than if no intervention had been attempted.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Pay-for-conservation schemes can create perverse incentives; discount ESG/biodiversity-credit claims without experimental evidence.
insights.quote: Paying Indonesian fishers for conservation actions actually made the problem worse.

insights.claim: The live-release payment was set near the market value of a retained fish, which the authors believe was too high for wedgefish, prompting fishers to fish harder in wedgefish areas.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Payment calibration relative to market value is the key design risk in incentive-based conservation.

insights.claim: Because hammerheads and wedgefish co-occur, extra effort targeting wedgefish also raised hammerhead catch; wedgefish (up to 90% survive capture) could be released for payment, but only about half of hammerheads survive, leaving dead ones to be sold at market.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Biological survival rates determine whether release incentives work; species-specific design matters.
insights.quote: A fisher who hauls up a dead hammerhead has no live-release video to submit and no payment to claim
insights.locator: The authors think they set the payment

insights.claim: The wedgefish effect was statistically insignificant, yet it is the key to explaining the hammerhead backfire, and the explanation relies on indirect evidence.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Mechanism for the backfire remains inferred, so treat causal story with caution.

insights.claim: Pay-to-release programs already operate in India, Brazil and other countries, and the Indonesian backfire shows conservation interventions should be experimentally evaluated before scale-up.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Existing pay-to-release programs may be net-harmful; donors and blended-finance conservation funds face evaluation risk.
insights.quote: conservation interventions should be experimentally evaluated before they are scaled up

insights.claim: Conservation effects likely differ by intervention design, economic environment and target species, which argues for a culture of experiments in environmental programs.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Generalising conservation results across settings is risky; demand site-specific evidence.

insights.claim: Booth et al. (2025) is the first experimental evidence on any ocean wildlife conservation intervention, unlike development economics where RCTs are common.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Marine conservation spending runs almost entirely without causal evidence, a governance gap for impact investors.
insights.quote: wildlife conservation is not like development economics

insights.claim: Running conservation RCTs is logistically far harder than causal inference with secondary data, but researchers willing to manage field teams face a near-empty evidence landscape with good publication prospects and high policy impact.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Opportunity for funders to back conservation experiments with outsized policy leverage.
insights.quote: researchers with a greater appetite for managing field teams face a near-empty evidence landscape
